text:
LAG positive: reitsma bivariate model meta-analysis (sensitivity and specificity)

Comparison: Index test

Methods

Sensitivity and specificity estimates were pooled using a reitsma bivariate model model. Meta-regression was performed with Dose as moderators. A continuity correction of 0.5 was applied to All studies if any zero exists. Analyses were performed in RC MetaStudio 0.5.1. R packages loaded for this analysis: metafor 5.0.1, meta 8.5-0, mada 0.5.12.

Results

17 studies were included.

No structured pooled estimates are available for this workflow; the complete output is in Supplementary details.

Table 1. Model fit

Statistic	Value

Studies (k)	17

Participants	1408

No study-level estimates or weights are available for this workflow.

text:
LAG positive: reitsma bivariate model meta-analysis (sensitivity and specificity)

Comparison: Index test

Methods

Sensitivity and specificity estimates were pooled using a reitsma bivariate model model. Meta-regression was performed with Group as moderators. A continuity correction of 0.5 was applied to All studies if any zero exists. Analyses were performed in RC MetaStudio 0.5.1. R packages loaded for this analysis: metafor 5.0.1, meta 8.5-0, mada 0.5.12.

Results

17 studies were included.

No structured pooled estimates are available for this workflow; the complete output is in Supplementary details.

LAG positive: reitsma bivariate model meta-analysis (sensitivity and specificity)

Comparison: Index test

Methods

Sensitivity and specificity estimates were pooled using a reitsma bivariate model model. Meta-regression was performed with Group as moderators. A continuity correction of 0.5 was applied to All studies if any zero exists. Analyses were performed in RC MetaStudio 0.5.1. R packages loaded for this analysis: metafor 5.0.1, meta 8.5-0, mada 0.5.12.

17 studies were included.

text:
LAG positive: reitsma bivariate model meta-analysis (sensitivity and specificity)

Comparison: Index test

Methods

Sensitivity and specificity estimates were pooled using a reitsma bivariate model model. Meta-regression was performed with Group, Dose as moderators. A continuity correction of 0.5 was applied to All studies if any zero exists. Analyses were performed in RC MetaStudio 0.5.1. R packages loaded for this analysis: metafor 5.0.1, meta 8.5-0, mada 0.5.12.

Results

17 studies were included.

text:
LAG positive: reitsma bivariate model meta-analysis (sensitivity and specificity)

Comparison: Index test

Methods

Sensitivity and specificity estimates were pooled using a reitsma bivariate model model. Meta-regression was performed with Group, Dose as moderators. A continuity correction of 0.5 was applied to All studies if any zero exists. Analyses were performed in RC MetaStudio 0.5.1. R packages loaded for this analysis: metafor 5.0.1, meta 8.5-0, mada 0.5.12.

Results

17 studies were included.

No structured pooled estimates are available for this workflow; the complete output is in Supplementary details.

text:
LAG positive: random-effects meta-analysis (diagnostic odds ratio)

Comparison: Index test

Methods

Diagnostic odds ratio estimates were pooled using a random-effects model with the DerSimonian–Laird estimator of between-study variance. Confidence intervals (95%) used the normal approximation. Cumulative meta-analysis was performed in current study order. A continuity correction of 0.5 was applied to studies with any zero cell. Analyses were performed in RC MetaStudio 0.5.1. R packages loaded for this analysis: metafor 5.0.1, meta 8.5-0, mada 0.5.12.

Results

17 studies were included. The pooled diagnostic odds ratio was 153.90 (95% CI [18.56, 1276.37]). The pooled diagnostic odds ratio was 28.26 (95% CI [1.14, 703.74], p = .042). The pooled diagnostic odds ratio was 49.83 (95% CI [5.06, 491.07], p < .001). The pooled diagnostic odds ratio was 47.82 (95% CI [8.52, 268.53], p < .001). The pooled diagnostic odds ratio was 25.97 (95% CI [4.46, 151.11], p < .001). The pooled diagnostic odds ratio was 24.37 (95% CI [5.63, 105.52], p < .001). The pooled diagnostic odds ratio was 19.35 (95% CI [5.31, 70.46], p < .001). The pooled diagnostic odds ratio was 14.18 (95% CI [5.18, 38.86], p < .001). The pooled diagnostic odds ratio was 11.49 (95% CI [4.89, 27.02], p < .001). The pooled diagnostic odds ratio was 10.65 (95% CI [4.87, 23.31], p < .001). The pooled diagnostic odds ratio was 9.34 (95% CI [4.69, 18.60], p < .001). The pooled diagnostic odds ratio was 10.64 (95% CI [5.36, 21.09], p < .001). The pooled diagnostic odds ratio was 9.37 (95% CI [4.83, 18.18], p < .001). The pooled diagnostic odds ratio was 8.41 (95% CI [4.54, 15.60], p < .001). The pooled diagnostic odds ratio was 8.38 (95% CI [4.82, 14.55], p < .001). The pooled diagnostic odds ratio was 9.33 (95% CI [5.30, 16.42], p < .001). The pooled diagnostic odds ratio was 9.65 (95% CI [5.53, 16.84], p < .001).

text:
LAG positive: random-effects meta-analysis (diagnostic odds ratio)

Comparison: Index test

Methods

Diagnostic odds ratio estimates were pooled using a random-effects model with the DerSimonian–Laird estimator of between-study variance. Confidence intervals (95%) used the normal approximation. Subgroup analyses were performed by Group. Subgroup differences were tested using heterogeneity Q among the subgroup estimates, weighted by their inverse variances. A continuity correction of 0.5 was applied to studies with any zero cell. Analyses were performed in RC MetaStudio 0.5.1. R packages loaded for this analysis: metafor 5.0.1, meta 8.5-0, mada 0.5.12.

Results

17 studies were included. In Subgroup B, the pooled diagnostic odds ratio was 9.01 (95% CI [4.10, 19.81], z = 5.47, p < .001). In Subgroup A, the pooled diagnostic odds ratio was 10.88 (95% CI [4.67, 25.33], z = 5.53, p < .001). Overall, the pooled diagnostic odds ratio was 9.65 (95% CI [5.53, 16.84], z = 7.98, p < .001). Subgroup B: Heterogeneity: Q = 26.73, df = 8, p < .001. Subgroup B: I² = 70.1%, which may represent substantial heterogeneity (Cochrane Handbook ranges). Subgroup B: Between-study variance was τ² = 0.83. Subgroup A: Heterogeneity: Q = 14.83, df = 7, p = .038. Subgroup A: I² = 52.8%, which may represent moderate to substantial heterogeneity (Cochrane Handbook ranges). Subgroup A: Between-study variance was τ² = 0.74. Overall: Heterogeneity: Q = 42.26, df = 16, p < .001. Overall: I² = 62.1%, which may represent substantial heterogeneity (Cochrane Handbook ranges). Overall: Between-study variance was τ² = 0.70. Subgroup B: The 95% prediction interval was 1.28 to 63.50. Subgroup A: The 95% prediction interval was 1.65 to 71.50. Overall: The 95% prediction interval was 1.70 to 54.78. Test for subgroup differences: Q = 0.10, df = 1, p = .750.

text:
Verification outcome: random-effects meta-analysis (odds ratio)

Comparison: Drug / Control

Methods

Odds ratios were pooled using a random-effects model with the DerSimonian–Laird estimator of between-study variance. Confidence intervals (95%) used the normal approximation. Heterogeneity was assessed with Cochran's Q and I². Analyses were performed in RC MetaStudio 0.5.1. R packages loaded for this analysis: metafor 5.0.1, meta 8.5-0, mada 0.5.12.

Results

6 studies were included (135 participants in Drug, 147 in Control). The pooled odds ratio was 0.761368 (95% CI [0.458516, 1.264253], z = -1.053719, p = .292). The confidence interval includes 1, so these data do not show a clear difference between Drug and Control. Heterogeneity: Q = 0.065861, df = 5, p = 1.000. I² = 0.0%, which may represent heterogeneity that might not be important (Cochrane Handbook ranges). Between-study variance was τ² = 0.000000. The 95% prediction interval was 0.458516 to 1.264253.

text:
Verification outcome: random-effects meta-analysis (odds ratio)

Comparison: Drug / Control

Methods

Odds ratios were pooled using a random-effects model with the DerSimonian–Laird estimator of between-study variance. Confidence intervals (95%) used the normal approximation. Heterogeneity was assessed with Cochran's Q and I². Analyses were performed in RC MetaStudio 0.5.1. R packages loaded for this analysis: metafor 5.0.1, meta 8.5-0, mada 0.5.12.

Results

6 studies were included (135 participants in Drug, 147 in Control). The pooled odds ratio was 0.761368 (95% CI [0.458516, 1.264253], z = -1.053719, p = .292). The confidence interval includes 1, so these data do not show a clear difference between Drug and Control. Heterogeneity: Q = 0.065861, df = 5, p = 1.000. I² = 0.0%, which may represent heterogeneity that might not be important (Cochrane Handbook ranges). Between-study variance was τ² = 0.000000. The 95% prediction interval was 0.458516 to 1.264253.

text:
Verification outcome: random-effects meta-analysis (odds ratio)

Comparison: Cognitive behavioural therapy plus usual care / Usual care only

Methods

Odds ratios were pooled using a random-effects model with the DerSimonian–Laird estimator of between-study variance. Confidence intervals (95%) used the normal approximation. Heterogeneity was assessed with Cochran's Q and I². Analyses were performed in RC MetaStudio 0.5.1. R packages loaded for this analysis: metafor 5.0.1, meta 8.5-0, mada 0.5.12.

Results

6 studies were included (135 participants in Cognitive behavioural therapy plus usual care, 147 in Usual care only). The pooled odds ratio was 0.761368 (95% CI [0.458516, 1.264253], z = -1.053719, p = .292). The confidence interval includes 1, so these data do not show a clear difference between Cognitive behavioural therapy plus usual care and Usual care only. Heterogeneity: Q = 0.065861, df = 5, p = 1.000. I² = 0.0%, which may represent heterogeneity that might not be important (Cochrane Handbook ranges). Between-study variance was τ² = 0.000000. The 95% prediction interval was 0.458516 to 1.264253.

text:
Verification outcome: random-effects meta-analysis (odds ratio)

Comparison: Cognitive behavioural therapy plus usual care / Usual care only

Methods

Odds ratios were pooled using a random-effects model with the DerSimonian–Laird estimator of between-study variance. Confidence intervals (95%) used the normal approximation. Heterogeneity was assessed with Cochran's Q and I². Analyses were performed in RC MetaStudio 0.5.1. R packages loaded for this analysis: metafor 5.0.1, meta 8.5-0, mada 0.5.12.

Results

6 studies were included (135 participants in Cognitive behavioural therapy plus usual care, 147 in Usual care only). The pooled odds ratio was 0.761368 (95% CI [0.458516, 1.264253], z = -1.053719, p = .292). The confidence interval includes 1, so these data do not show a clear difference between Cognitive behavioural therapy plus usual care and Usual care only. Heterogeneity: Q = 0.065861, df = 5, p = 1.000. I² = 0.0%, which may represent heterogeneity that might not be important (Cochrane Handbook ranges). Between-study variance was τ² = 0.000000. The 95% prediction interval was 0.458516 to 1.264253.

text:
Verification outcome: random-effects meta-analysis (odds ratio)

Comparison: Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-up / Standard clinical care

Methods

Odds ratios were pooled using a random-effects model with the DerSimonian–Laird estimator of between-study variance. Confidence intervals (95%) used the normal approximation. Heterogeneity was assessed with Cochran's Q and I². Analyses were performed in RC MetaStudio 0.5.1. R packages loaded for this analysis: metafor 5.0.1, meta 8.5-0, mada 0.5.12.

Results

6 studies were included (135 participants in Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-up, 147 in Standard clinical care). The pooled odds ratio was 0.761368 (95% CI [0.458516, 1.264253], z = -1.053719, p = .292). The confidence interval includes 1, so these data do not show a clear difference between Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-up and Standard clinical care. Heterogeneity: Q = 0.065861, df = 5, p = 1.000. I² = 0.0%, which may represent heterogeneity that might not be important (Cochrane Handbook ranges). Between-study variance was τ² = 0.000000. The 95% prediction interval was 0.458516 to 1.264253.

text:
Verification outcome: random-effects meta-analysis (odds ratio)

Comparison: Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-up / Standard clinical care

Methods

Odds ratios were pooled using a random-effects model with the DerSimonian–Laird estimator of between-study variance. Confidence intervals (95%) used the normal approximation. Heterogeneity was assessed with Cochran's Q and I². Analyses were performed in RC MetaStudio 0.5.1. R packages loaded for this analysis: metafor 5.0.1, meta 8.5-0, mada 0.5.12.

Results

6 studies were included (135 participants in Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-up, 147 in Standard clinical care). The pooled odds ratio was 0.761368 (95% CI [0.458516, 1.264253], z = -1.053719, p = .292). The confidence interval includes 1, so these data do not show a clear difference between Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-up and Standard clinical care. Heterogeneity: Q = 0.065861, df = 5, p = 1.000. I² = 0.0%, which may represent heterogeneity that might not be important (Cochrane Handbook ranges). Between-study variance was τ² = 0.000000. The 95% prediction interval was 0.458516 to 1.264253.

text:
Verification outcome: random-effects meta-analysis (odds ratio)

Comparison: Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-up / Standard clinical care

Methods

Odds ratios were pooled using a random-effects model with the DerSimonian–Laird estimator of between-study variance. Confidence intervals (95%) used the normal approximation. Heterogeneity was assessed with Cochran's Q and I². Analyses were performed in RC MetaStudio 0.5.1. R packages loaded for this analysis: metafor 5.0.1, meta 8.5-0, mada 0.5.12.

Results

6 studies were included (135 participants in Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-up, 147 in Standard clinical care). The pooled odds ratio was 0.761368 (95% CI [0.458516, 1.264253], z = -1.053719, p = .292). The confidence interval includes 1, so these data do not show a clear difference between Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-up and Standard clinical care. Heterogeneity: Q = 0.065861, df = 5, p = 1.000. I² = 0.0%, which may represent heterogeneity that might not be important (Cochrane Handbook ranges). Between-study variance was τ² = 0.000000. The 95% prediction interval was 0.458516 to 1.264253.

text:
Verification outcome: random-effects meta-analysis (odds ratio)

Comparison: Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-up / Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-through

Methods

Odds ratios were pooled using a random-effects model with the DerSimonian–Laird estimator of between-study variance. Confidence intervals (95%) used the normal approximation. Heterogeneity was assessed with Cochran's Q and I². Analyses were performed in RC MetaStudio 0.5.1. R packages loaded for this analysis: metafor 5.0.1, meta 8.5-0, mada 0.5.12.

Results

6 studies were included (135 participants in Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-up, 147 in Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-through). The pooled odds ratio was 0.761368 (95% CI [0.458516, 1.264253], z = -1.053719, p = .292). The confidence interval includes 1, so these data do not show a clear difference between Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-up and Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-through. Heterogeneity: Q = 0.065861, df = 5, p = 1.000. I² = 0.0%, which may represent heterogeneity that might not be important (Cochrane Handbook ranges). Between-study variance was τ² = 0.000000. The 95% prediction interval was 0.458516 to 1.264253.

text:
Verification outcome: random-effects meta-analysis (odds ratio)

Comparison: Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-up / Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-through

Methods

Odds ratios were pooled using a random-effects model with the DerSimonian–Laird estimator of between-study variance. Confidence intervals (95%) used the normal approximation. Heterogeneity was assessed with Cochran's Q and I². Analyses were performed in RC MetaStudio 0.5.1. R packages loaded for this analysis: metafor 5.0.1, meta 8.5-0, mada 0.5.12.

Results

6 studies were included (135 participants in Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-up, 147 in Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-through). The pooled odds ratio was 0.761368 (95% CI [0.458516, 1.264253], z = -1.053719, p = .292). The confidence interval includes 1, so these data do not show a clear difference between Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-up and Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-through. Heterogeneity: Q = 0.065861, df = 5, p = 1.000. I² = 0.0%, which may represent heterogeneity that might not be important (Cochrane Handbook ranges). Between-study variance was τ² = 0.000000. The 95% prediction interval was 0.458516 to 1.264253.

text:
Verification outcome: random-effects meta-analysis (odds ratio)

Comparison: Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-up / Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-through

Methods

Odds ratios were pooled using a random-effects model with the DerSimonian–Laird estimator of between-study variance. Confidence intervals (95%) used the normal approximation. Heterogeneity was assessed with Cochran's Q and I². Analyses were performed in RC MetaStudio 0.5.1. R packages loaded for this analysis: metafor 5.0.1, meta 8.5-0, mada 0.5.12.

Results

6 studies were included (135 participants in Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-up, 147 in Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-through). The pooled odds ratio was 0.761368 (95% CI [0.458516, 1.264253], z = -1.053719, p = .292). The confidence interval includes 1, so these data do not show a clear difference between Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-up and Intensive individualized cognitive behavioural therapy plus structured clinical follow-through. Heterogeneity: Q = 0.065861, df = 5, p = 1.000. I² = 0.0%, which may represent heterogeneity that might not be important (Cochrane Handbook ranges). Between-study variance was τ² = 0.000000. The 95% prediction interval was 0.458516 to 1.264253.
